html:
Dʿmt, labelled Damot on the map, was a kingdom in the highlands of what is now Eritrea and northern Ethiopia in the first millennium BCE, before Aksum. The map shows it in 300 BCE, but its known inscriptions and buildings date mostly from about the 8th to the 5th centuries BCE, and little is known of it after that.

Its centre was probably at Yeha, where a tall stone temple still stands. The kingdom had close ties with Saba across the Red Sea in southern Arabia. Its kings wrote in a South Arabian script, used South Arabian gods and building styles, and may have included settlers from Arabia, though most people were local highland farmers growing cereals and keeping cattle.

After Dʿmt broke up, smaller states held the region until Aksum rose in the first centuries CE, and the Ge'ez script of Ethiopia grew out of the writing of this period. The name Damot also belongs to a different, later kingdom further south in Ethiopia, which fought the Christian kings in the 1200s; the map's label refers to the older northern state.
